why: Barcelona ships 6 image placements across 35 pages (17% of pages carry a photograph). The fleet band is 45-74%. Sixteen more plates bring it to roughly the fleet median. Each slot names what the plate must DO on that page, because a plate that only decorates costs a third of a sheet and argues nothing.
target: 3:2 landscape, >=1600px wide, no identifiable faces, no legible brand signage in the foreground

slots.title: Before You Fly
slots.brief: A Barcelona hotel or apartment front door in the Eixample — the plain modernista entrance with its wrought-iron and tile, shot straight on in flat morning light. The chapter is about deadlines and bookings, so the plate should read as the thing you are booking, not as a sight.

slots.title: Day Zero
slots.brief: The airport metro platform or a T-casual validation gate at El Prat — signage legible, no faces. This chapter's single most expensive fact is the airport ticket, and the plate should show the gate where it gets discovered too late.

slots.title: Timing
slots.brief: A Barcelona street in low shoulder-season light — long shadows, a plaça with locals rather than queues, trees still in leaf. Must NOT look like high summer: the chapter's call is May–June and September–October, and the picture has to argue for that light.

slots.title: The Set Pieces
slots.brief: The Sagrada Família nave interior with morning sun through the east windows — the gold-and-amber cast, columns receding. This is the image that justifies the morning-slot call; an exterior shot of the façade does not.

slots.title: The Apartment Question
slots.brief: A Barcelona balcony row with a visible tourist-apartment licence plaque, or a residential Eixample stairwell. The chapter is about a licence regime being withdrawn, so the plate wants ordinary residential fabric, not a styled interior.

slots.title: The Money-Trap Web
slots.brief: A card terminal held out across a café table, or a standalone blue ATM on a tourist street. The four traps all happen at a point of sale; the plate should be a point of sale.

slots.title: Sequencing the Days
slots.brief: A timed-entry queue at a Gaudí site, seen from behind, with the hour visibly early — thin crowd, raking light. The chapter argues that the same ticket is a different experience at a different hour, and the plate should be the good hour.

slots.title: The Horizons
slots.brief: A booking-relevant Barcelona surface: a ticket office window, a timetable board, an FGC platform at Plaça d'Espanya. The chapter is about what binds and when, so the plate should show a schedule or a counter rather than scenery.

slots.title: How Worried Should You Be?
slots.brief: La Rambla or a metro carriage in ordinary daylight, crowded but unremarkable, no faces identifiable. The chapter's whole argument is proportion: the picture must look mundane, NOT menacing — a dramatic night shot would contradict the text.

slots.title: The Plan
slots.brief: A wide Barcelona rooftop or Montjuïc view showing the Eixample grid running to the sea, so the reader can see the geometry the five-day shape is built on. This is the one place a panorama earns its space.

slots.title: Failure Modes
slots.brief: A closed gate, a sold-out sign, or an empty grey beach — one image of a day that did not work. The chapter is organised by consequence, and the plate should carry the cost rather than the city.

slots.title: The Wallet Card
slots.brief: A hand holding a phone or a printed card at a counter — the moment of use. This chapter is the on-the-trip document; the plate should show it being used, not the city.

slots.title: Decide these first
slots.brief: A desk with a laptop, a calendar and a notebook — the pre-trip planning surface, at home rather than in Barcelona. This spread is read before you leave, and the plate should say so.

slots.title: What This Won't Tell You
slots.brief: A quiet, unlabelled Barcelona street with no landmark in it — the version of the city the book explicitly refuses to name for you. Anonymity is the point.

slots.title: The Contract
slots.brief: A Barcelona street sign or a tiled street name plate, shot tight. The opening chapter is about how to think rather than what to see, so the plate should be a detail, not a monument.

slots.title: Which Day Trip (second plate)
slots.brief: Montserrat's serrated rock spires with the monastery small against them, from the cable car or the approach. A05 already carries a general day-trip plate; this is the one that makes the Montserrat call visible.
